869.title: Ashvamedhika
869.hook: a sage in the desert hears the war is over and threatens to curse Krishna for not stopping it
869.carry: because of who was holding the cup
869.howItsDone: Uttanka's meeting with Krishna is told in the Ashvamedhika Parva, and storytellers retell the episode of Indra's disguised gift as a lesson about judging people by appearance.

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna admitted he'd forgotten the Gita, and Krishna taught again through old stories, the Anugita. Your line was I've forgotten it.

Krishna is heading home to Dwaraka across a desert when he meets an old friend: the sage Uttanka, who has spent a long time in austerity and hasn't heard the news. Uttanka greets him warmly. So, did you make peace between the cousins? Krishna tells him the truth. There was no peace. The Kauravas are dead. And the sage's face changes. You could have stopped it, Uttanka says, and you didn't. He raises his hand to curse the man standing in front of him.
screen: `A SAGE IN THE DESERT.` → `"DID YOU MAKE PEACE?"` → `HE RAISES HIS HAND TO CURSE.`

segments.voice: Krishna doesn't flinch, and he doesn't argue first. Hear me out, he says, and then decide. He tells Uttanka that he tried, that he went to the Kauravas himself, and they would not listen. Then he speaks of his own nature and, in the epic's telling, shows Uttanka the same vast universal form Arjuna saw before the battle. The sage lowers his hand. Krishna offers him a gift, and Uttanka, who lives in this dry country, asks for something simple: water, whenever he needs it. Think of me, Krishna says, and you'll have it. Some time later Uttanka is wandering, desperately thirsty, and he remembers. And who comes toward him? A hunter, an outcast by the rules of the time, filthy, surrounded by dogs, offering him water. Uttanka is disgusted, refuses, and sends the man away. Then Krishna appears and explains. That was Indra, king of the gods. Krishna had asked him to bring Uttanka amrita, the drink of immortality. Indra agreed, but chose to bring it in that form, to see what the sage would do. And Uttanka turned it down because of who was holding the cup. The angry sage who judged Krishna by the outcome of a war has just judged a gift by the look of its giver. Krishna still gives him something: clouds that will rain water for him in the desert whenever he thinks of them.
screen: `"HEAR ME OUT FIRST"` · `THE BOON: WATER IN THE DESERT` · `AN OUTCAST HUNTER OFFERS A DRINK` · then, large: `IT WAS INDRA, CARRYING AMRITA`

segments.voice: Let your breath slow and bring to mind someone whose help you'd refuse because of who they are, how they look, or what they once did. Without changing your mind about them, picture them holding out something you need, and notice honestly what rises in you. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer, just as they are.

870.title: Ashvamedhika
870.hook: Abhimanyu's son is born without breath, and the women of the house turn to Krishna
870.carry: a kept promise, a true sentence
870.howItsDone: Parikshit's revival is told in the Ashvamedhika Parva, and Hindu tradition remembers Parikshit as the king to whom, in the Bhagavata Purana, the sage Shuka later recites that text.

segments.voice: Yesterday Uttanka refused water from an outcast hunter who turned out to be Indra, carrying amrita. Your line was because of who was holding the cup.

After the night raid, Ashvatthama loosed a terrible weapon he couldn't call back, and turned it on the wombs of the Pandava women. Krishna answered him then with a promise: the child Uttara is carrying will live. Now the Pandavas are away in the mountains, fetching Marutta's gold. Uttara, Abhimanyu's young widow, goes into labor. The child is born, and he doesn't breathe. Kunti, Draupadi, Subhadra and Uttara herself are in that room. The promise is called in.
screen: `ASHVATTHAMA'S WEAPON.` → `KRISHNA'S PROMISE.` → `A CHILD BORN WITHOUT BREATH.`

segments.voice: The grief here is not quiet. Kunti, Abhimanyu's grandmother, reminds Krishna of his words: you promised this child would live. Subhadra, Krishna's own sister and Abhimanyu's mother, pleads with him. And Uttara speaks to the still baby in her arms, in Ganguli's telling, as if he could hear: your father died young, and now you have gone after him. Krishna goes into the birth room. He doesn't bargain or chant a spell. He makes a declaration of truth. In this tradition, a true statement, solemnly spoken, has power. Krishna names truths about his own life: that he has not spoken a falsehood, not even in jest, that he has not turned his back in battle, that righteousness is dear to him. By the force of those truths, he says, let this child live. The child stirs, and breathes. The house that was wailing fills with joy. This boy is Parikshit, and the dynasty that was nearly erased will go on through him. Later he'll be king. Look where the life comes from in this scene: not a weapon, not a trick, but a life lived truthfully, spoken out loud when it's needed. During the war, a half-truth from Yudhishthira brought Drona down. Here, at the cradle, a kept promise and a true sentence bring a child back.
screen: `KUNTI: "YOU PROMISED"` · `UTTARA SPEAKS TO HER SON` · `A DECLARATION OF TRUTH` · then, large: `PARIKSHIT BREATHES`

871.title: Ashvamedhika
871.hook: the sacrificial horse reaches Manipura, and the young king who comes out to meet Arjuna is his own son
871.carry: the fight he demanded set him free
871.howItsDone: Arjuna's encounter with Babhruvahana is told in the Ashvamedhika Parva, and the episode is remembered in Manipur and retold in Indian theater and storytelling.

segments.voice: Yesterday a child born without breath lived, by Krishna's declaration of truth. His name is Parikshit. Your line was a kept promise, a true sentence.

The horse has been set loose at last. It wanders where it likes, and Arjuna follows with his bow, country after country, fighting the kings who challenge it. Then it walks into Manipura. Long ago, on his travels, Arjuna married a princess of this land, Chitrangada, and left a son here. That son, Babhruvahana, is king now. And he comes out of the city to meet the horse, not with an army but with gifts and brahmanas, his head bowed to his father.
screen: `THE HORSE WANDERS.` → `IT ENTERS MANIPURA.` → `HIS SON COMES OUT WITH GIFTS.`

segments.voice: Arjuna is angry. In Ganguli's telling he scolds his son: I've come here guarding a sacrificial horse, as a warrior, and you greet me like this? A king of your order should come out and fight. Babhruvahana stands there, humiliated. Then someone rises out of the earth: Ulupi, the serpent princess, another of Arjuna's wives from those travels. Do what your father asks, she tells the young king. Fight him. So he arms himself, and father and son meet in battle, and the son is very good. His arrow strikes Arjuna, and Arjuna falls and does not get up. Seeing what he has done, Babhruvahana collapses too. Chitrangada runs onto the field and finds her husband dead and her son unconscious. She turns on Ulupi: this is your doing. Babhruvahana wakes and vows to fast until he dies beside his father. Then Ulupi does the second strange thing. She brings out a gem from the serpent world, a jewel that restores life, and places it on Arjuna's chest. He wakes as if from sleep. Ulupi explains. When Arjuna brought Bhishma down from behind Shikhandi, the Vasus, Bhishma's divine brothers, cursed him. Her father pleaded for him, and the answer was that the curse would end at the hands of his own son. Today it did. The fight Arjuna demanded is the one that set him free.
screen: `ARJUNA SCOLDS HIS SON` · `ULUPI: "FIGHT HIM"` · `THE SON'S ARROW FELLS THE FATHER` · then, large: `A GEM, AND AN OLD CURSE LIFTED`

872.title: Ashvamedhika
872.hook: the great sacrifice is finished and praised by all, and a mongoose with half a golden body says it isn't worth a handful of flour
872.tomorrow: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven
872.howItsDone: The story of the mongoose and the gleaner's flour closes the account of Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice in the Ashvamedhika Parva, and storytellers retell it to teach that a gift given in want outweighs great display.

segments.voice: Yesterday at Manipura, Arjuna was struck down by his own son, and Ulupi's gem brought him back. Your line was the fight he demanded set him free.

Gold handed out to the brahmanas, food for everyone, kings and sages crowding the grounds: the horse is home, the sacrifice is done, and everyone says there's never been a rite like it. Then, from a hole in the ground, out comes a mongoose. One side of its body is gold. It looks around at all this splendor and speaks, in a voice like thunder: this sacrifice of yours isn't equal to a little barley flour given away by a poor brahmana in Kurukshetra. The crowd goes silent.
screen: `THE SACRIFICE IS DONE.` → `A MONGOOSE, HALF GOLD.` → `"NOT EQUAL TO A LITTLE FLOUR."`

segments.voice: The brahmanas ask the mongoose to explain. In Kurukshetra, it says, there lived a brahmana who fed his family by gleaning, picking up the grains left in the fields after harvest. A famine came, and the family went hungry for a long time. At last he gathered enough barley for a little flour, and they divided it among the four of them: the man, his wife, their son and the son's wife. Just as they were about to eat, a hungry guest arrived. The brahmana welcomed him and gave him his own share. The guest ate it and was still hungry. The wife gave hers. Then the son. Then the daughter-in-law. Every portion went to a stranger, while the family sat with nothing. Then the guest revealed himself: he was Dharma, righteousness itself. He praised the gift as greater than great sacrifices, and the family was carried to heaven. The mongoose had come out of its hole as this happened. It rolled in the scattered flour and the water where the guest had washed, and wherever the flour touched, its fur turned to gold. Half of it. Ever since, it says, it has gone from sacrifice to sacrifice, rolling on the ground, hoping to turn the other half gold. It just rolled in Yudhishthira's. Nothing changed. The epic puts this near the close of the book of a great royal rite. The verdict on the gold doesn't come from a priest. It comes from a small animal, and a handful of barley.
screen: `A GLEANER'S FAMILY IN FAMINE` · `FOUR SHARES, ALL GIVEN AWAY` · `THE GUEST WAS DHARMA` · then, large: `HALF GOLD, STILL ROLLING`

segments.voice: Rest your hands palms up in your lap, as if holding a small bowl, and think of your last meal, and of who else might have been hungry at that hour, letting the two thoughts sit side by side without guilt. Then think of one small portion, not grand, just real, that you could give; if you pray, you can offer that intention in your prayer.

Your line: a handful of barley. The mongoose is still rolling, half gold. See you tomorrow.

873.title: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven
873.hook: the kingdom is handed on, the brothers and Draupadi take off their ornaments and walk out of the city, and a dog follows them
873.tomorrow: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven
873.howItsDone: The Mahaprasthanika Parva tells the Pandavas' final walk; Hindus hear it in recitations of the epic, and the image of the brothers, Draupadi and the dog walking toward the Himalayas is often painted and retold.

segments.voice: Yesterday Ashvamedhika closed with a half-golden mongoose and a family's handful of flour. Between that book and today's, the epic tells of the elders' deaths in the forest and the end of Krishna's people. Your line was a handful of barley.

The news from Dwaraka reaches Hastinapura: Krishna is gone, and his clan has destroyed itself. Yudhishthira makes up his mind in one sentence, in Ganguli's telling: time is cooking all creatures. It's time to go. He crowns Parikshit, the child who was born without breath, now grown, and puts the kingdom in others' care. Then the five brothers and Draupadi take off their jewelry, put on the plain clothes of forest hermits, and walk out through the gates. The city follows a little way, weeping, and turns back. One companion does not turn back. A dog.
screen: `NEWS FROM DWARAKA.` → `PARIKSHIT IS CROWNED.` → `SIX WALK OUT, AND A DOG.`

segments.voice: This book is the Mahaprasthanika, the book of the great departure, and it has the feel of a last chapter. The Pandavas walk east first: Yudhishthira leads, then Bhima, Arjuna, the twins, Draupadi, and the dog behind them all. They reach the sea, and a figure stands in their path, tall as a mountain: Agni, the god of fire. He speaks to Arjuna. Remember the great bow Gandiva? Agni himself brought it to Arjuna long ago, from Varuna, lord of the waters. Now he asks for it back. Its work is finished; it belongs to Varuna; give it to the sea. And Arjuna, who carried that bow through the whole war, throws it into the waves, with his quivers that never ran empty. Arjuna the archer walks on unarmed. So the great departure starts not with a battle or a prayer, but with letting go of the thing you were best known for. The ornaments came off at the gate. The bow goes into the sea. The kingdom is in Parikshit's hands. Each step is lighter. Then the walk itself begins, around the edge of the world: south, then west, where they see the sea over the place Dwaraka stood, then north, toward the mountains. They are walking toward Meru, toward heaven, in their bodies, while they still have them. And the dog keeps coming.
screen: `MAHAPRASTHANIKA: THE GREAT DEPARTURE` · `AGNI STANDS AT THE SEA` · `"GIVE GANDIVA BACK TO VARUNA"` · then, large: `THE BOW GOES INTO THE WAVES`

segments.voice: Seven travelers climb into the Himalayas: five brothers, one queen, one dog. They cross the mountains and, beyond them, a great desert of sand, and far off they can see Meru, the mountain at the center of the world. They walk in single file, Yudhishthira in front, Draupadi near the back. Then, without warning, she drops to the ground. Bhima sees her fall. And the man at the front of the line keeps walking.

segments.voice: Bhima calls out to his elder brother. In Ganguli's telling, his question is simple: she never did anything wrong, so why has she fallen? Yudhishthira answers without stopping. She loved Arjuna more than the rest of us, he says. That is what she is paying for now. And he walks on, the text says, without looking at her. That's a hard sentence to sit with. Draupadi has been at the center of so much of this story. She was married to all five brothers. She was dragged into the dice hall and humiliated, and asked the question that shamed the whole hall. She lost her sons in the night raid. And at the end of the road, the reason given for her fall is that her heart leaned toward one husband. Readers argue about this moment, and the epic doesn't settle it. Some hear a strict, almost bookkeeping answer, the logic of the road: each falls by a small flaw, and nothing is hidden. Some notice that he never stops walking, never kneels, and ask what that costs him. And some point out that the epic isn't finished with this scene: Draupadi's fall is not the last word on Draupadi. We'll see her again. For now, there's a line of travelers getting shorter, and a question asked by the brother who stopped to look. Bhima turns back to the path. The dog keeps walking.

875.howItsDone: The falls of Sahadeva and Nakula are told in the Mahaprasthanika Parva, and Hindu teachers sometimes use the sequence of falls to talk about the small faults that weigh down even good people.

segments.voice: Yesterday Draupadi fell first in the sea of sand, and Bhima was the one who stopped to ask why. Your line was she loved Arjuna more than the rest of us.

Sahadeva and Nakula are the youngest of the five, the twins, sons of Madri, raised by Kunti as her own. In this serial they have often stood just behind their older brothers: Sahadeva, known for his learning; Nakula, known as the handsome one. Now, on the road toward Meru, Sahadeva falls. A little later, Nakula falls too. Both times Bhima calls out to the front of the line, and both times Yudhishthira answers without stopping.
screen: `THE TWINS, SONS OF MADRI.` → `SAHADEVA FALLS.` → `THEN NAKULA.`

segments.voice: Listen to the shape of the answers. About Sahadeva, in Ganguli's telling: he thought no one was equal to him in wisdom. About Nakula: he thought no one was equal to him in beauty. The same sentence twice, with one word changed. Look at what isn't blamed. Not the learning. Not the good looks. Those are gifts, and the epic has praised both brothers for them. What trips each of them is a small private thought laid on top of the gift: no one is equal to me. Sahadeva's wisdom could have walked on with him. What he couldn't carry to the top of the world, in this telling, was the comparison. The same goes for Nakula's face. Notice, too, who asks. Bhima, the strongest of them, calls out each time, and Yudhishthira answers only what he is asked. The pride he names isn't a boast spoken aloud. It's a quiet habit of measuring, held inside, and on a road this steep every extra ounce counts. Behind the line, the dog still walks. Three travelers are left with Yudhishthira now: Bhima, Arjuna and the dog. The road narrows as the people on it fall away, and the question Bhima keeps asking, why, gets the same kind of answer every time.
